text: You have n servers and a list of undirected connections. A connection is critical if removing it leaves some servers unable to reach some others. Return all critical connections.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — a critical connection is exactly a bridge: an edge whose removal raises the number of connected pieces. And an edge is a bridge if and only if it lies on no cycle — if it were on a cycle, I could still get across the other way. Is that the right framing?
Two quick constraints. Can the same pair appear twice — are there parallel edges? And is the graph guaranteed connected?
No repeated connections. Treat it as connected. n is up to ten to the fifth, and a similar number of edges.

Good — no parallel edges will matter later. Let me run through the example: zero-one, one-two, two-zero, and one-three. The zero, one, two triangle is one big cycle, so none of those three edges is a bridge. But one-three is the only way to reach three — cut it and three falls off. So the answer is just one-three.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to remove each edge, then run a BFS to see if the graph is still connected. That's E removals times V plus E per check — far too slow at a hundred thousand edges. This problem reminds me of Tarjan's bridge-finding. One DFS. I give each node a discovery time, dfn, and a value low — the earliest dfn the node's subtree can climb back to using one back edge. A tree edge u, v is a bridge exactly when low of v is greater than dfn of u: the subtree under v cannot reach u or anything above it, so that edge is its only way out.

Here's the plan. One: on visiting u, set both dfn and low to the next timer value. Two: for a tree edge, recurse, take the min with the child's low, and if low of v is greater than dfn of u, record a bridge. Three: for a back edge, take the min with dfn of v. One thing worth flagging — a back edge updates low with the neighbor's dfn, not its low, since it only proves I can reach that node. And the test is strict: if low of v equals dfn of u, the subtree can still climb back to u, so it's not a bridge. Also, I skip the parent by node, v equals p. That's only safe because there are no parallel edges; otherwise I'd skip by edge id. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. I build the adjacency list, set dfn and low to minus one for unvisited, and start a DFS from every unvisited node. Inside dfs, a tree edge recurses, pulls the child's low into mine, then tests low of v greater than dfn of u; a back edge only uses dfn of v. That matches the plan. One thing worth flagging — the root passes p equal to minus one. Since node ids run from zero to n minus one, that never equals a real neighbor, so the root's skip is a harmless no-op.

Let's dry-run the code with the example. I expect one-three. The row that matters is the return from node three. Node three has only its parent, one, as a neighbor, so low of three stays at three. Since three is greater than dfn of one, which is one, the edge one-three is its only exit — a bridge. Meanwhile, two's back edge to zero pulls low of two down to zero, so the triangle edges all fail the test. Corner cases: a straight chain — every edge is a bridge. A single cycle — no bridges. And the outer loop over unvisited nodes covers the graph even if it came in as more than one piece.

The time complexity is V plus E — one DFS touches every node and every edge once. The space complexity is V plus E, for the adjacency list, the two arrays, and the recursion stack. In the worst case a long chain makes the recursion depth V, so on a very deep graph I might switch to an explicit stack. Oh, one more thing — if the problem later allowed repeated connections, I'd move from the parent-node skip to an edge-id skip, and everything else stays the same.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You reframed critical connection as a bridge, an edge on no cycle, then as low of v greater than dfn of u. You were precise that a back edge uses dfn, not low, and that the test is strict. And you flagged that the simple parent skip is correct only because there are no parallel edges — with a clean upgrade path if that changed. Good work.
